title: Iris, child of Thaumas
greek: Thaumantias ... Iris, decus caeli
short: Juno sends Iris, the rainbow-messenger, to tell Turnus that Aeneas is away; Turnus recognises her as she leaves on her bow of light.
body: Iris is called Thaumantias, 'daughter of Thaumas', a sea-god whom Hesiod makes father of Iris and the Harpies (Theogony 265-269), as Conington notes. Her name is the Greek word for rainbow, and she 'flashed under the clouds in a long flying bow'. Turnus is found sitting in the sacred grove of his ancestor Pilumnus, an old Italian god (Conington explains that 'parent' here is used loosely, Pilumnus being his great-grandfather, 10.619). Turnus' prayer 'Iris, grace of the sky, who hath driven thee down?' echoes Achilles' question to Iris in Iliad 18.182, but, as Conington observes, Turnus gets no answer. Book IX thus opens with Turnus as an Achilles-figure, eager for battle and favoured by heaven, at the moment when his enemy is absent.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.5 (Thaumantias; and on 9.18, Il. 18.182)
Hesiod, Theogony 265-269 (Thaumas, father of Iris and the Harpies)
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.3 (parentis: Pilumnus)

title: Turnus as a wolf at the sheepfold
greek: ac veluti pleno lupus insidiatus ovili / cum fremit ad caulas ventos perpessus et imbris / nocte super media
short: Turnus riding round the walled Trojan camp is like a wolf howling at a full sheepfold at midnight, maddened by hunger and unable to get in.
body: The Trojans obey Aeneas' order not to fight in the open (9.40-43), so Turnus, the attacker, is frustrated: the lambs bleat 'safe beneath their mothers'. Conington identifies the main model as Apollonius Rhodius 1.1243 ff. and suggests Virgil also remembered Iliad 11.547 ff. (a lion kept from a fold by men and dogs) and Odyssey 6.130 ff. The details stress madness from long frustration: 'the long-gathering madness for food (edendi rabies), and the throat unslaked with blood'. Animal similes for Turnus multiply in Books IX-XII (wolf, tiger, lion); they make him heroic in energy but bestial in appetite. Compare the eagle and 'wolf of Mars' simile at 9.563-566.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.59 (Apollonius 1.1243 ff.; Il. 11.547 ff.)
Homer, Iliad 11.548 (lion kept from the fold)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.59, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Cybele, the Berecyntian Mother, and the sacred ships
greek: ipsa deum fertur genetrix Berecyntia magnum / vocibus his adfata Iovem
short: When Turnus tries to burn the Trojan fleet, Virgil tells how Cybele, Mother of the Gods, had given her sacred pines on Mount Ida to build it.
body: Cybele, the great Mother goddess of Phrygia, was worshipped on Mount Berecyntus and Mount Ida; Rome brought her cult from Asia Minor in 204 BC, and she had a temple on the Palatine near Augustus' house. Conington cross-refers to 6.784, where Rome itself is compared to the 'Berecyntian Mother' crowned with towers. She addresses Jupiter as her son ('Grant, O son'), recalling that she helped him win Olympus from his father. The episode opens with a fresh invocation of the Muses (9.77-79), signalling that what follows is a marvel needing divine authority: 'ancient is the assurance thereof, but the fame everlasting'. Numanus later mocks the Trojans as votaries of this Phrygian goddess (9.617-620).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.82 (Berecyntia; and on 9.84, domito Olympo)
Virgil, Aeneid 6.784 (Rome as the Berecyntian Mother), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 29.14 (the Magna Mater brought to Rome, 204 BC)

title: Jupiter's nod and the oath by the Styx
greek: Stygii per flumina fratris ... / adnuit et totum nutu tremefecit Olympum
short: Jupiter confirms his promise by nodding, swearing by the Styx, his brother Pluto's river, and the nod makes all Olympus tremble.
body: Conington explains that Virgil combines two Homeric ideas: Zeus' nod, the most binding pledge he can give (Iliad 1.524-530, where his nod shakes great Olympus), and the oath by the Styx, which binds the gods. The same line recurs at 10.115, where Jupiter again seals a decree. Jupiter will not make mortal ships immortal outright, since 'may hulls have the right of immortality that were fashioned by mortal hand?' (a nice theological point about the limits even on a god). Instead, after their service, those that reach Italy will become sea-nymphs. This preserves the rule of fate while granting Cybele's prayer.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.104 (Stygii per flumina fratris; Il. 1.525, 1.530)
Homer, Iliad 1.524 (Zeus' nod shakes Olympus)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.104, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: The ships turned into sea-nymphs
greek: inde (nova monstrum!) virgineae se totidem facies attollunt pelagoque feruntur
short: As Turnus' men bring fire, a great light and a voice from heaven release the Trojan ships, which plunge like dolphins and rise as sea-nymphs.
body: Ancient critics found this the most fantastic episode in the Aeneid; some modern readers have shared their discomfort. Virgil seems aware of the problem and anchors it in tradition with an invocation and the phrase 'ancient is the assurance thereof' (prisca fides facto, 9.79). Jupiter compares the new goddesses to the Nereids Doto and Galatea, names Conington traces to the list of Nereids in Iliad 18.39 ff. The miracle has a point: it shows the Trojans have finished their voyages, and their link with the sea is over. Turnus, characteristically, reads the portent against the Trojans: 'they have lost half their world'. Ovid retells the transformation (Met. 14.527-565). One ship-nymph, Cymodocea, returns at 10.219-248 to warn Aeneas.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.102 (Doto and Galatea; Il. 18.39 ff.)
Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.527-565 (the ships become nymphs)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.107, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Turnus' counter-fate
greek: sunt et mea contra / fata mihi, ferro sceleratam exscindere gentem / coniuge praerepta
short: Turnus answers the Trojans' fate with his own: to destroy the nation that has robbed him of his bride, as the Atreidae avenged the theft of Helen.
body: Turnus' speech is bold and clever. He casts himself as Menelaus and the Trojans as Paris' people, repeating the analogy Juno and Amata used (7.319-322, 7.363-364). Conington notes that he takes fata as 'destiny', and that Servius thought the claim false but allowable in rhetoric; Conington compares Hector's defiance of omens in Iliad 12.243. Turnus mocks the Greeks' methods at Troy: he needs no Vulcanian arms, no thousand ships, no wooden horse, no night-theft of the Palladium, and will fight in daylight. His contempt for trickery and his claim to fight openly make him attractive; but the speech also shows his blindness to divine signs that the reader has just witnessed.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.137 (fata; Servius; Il. 12.243)

Virgil, Aeneid 9.136, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

anchor: These two were one in affection
title: Nisus and Euryalus
greek: his amor unus erat pariterque in bella ruebant
short: Nisus and Euryalus, already known from the foot-race of Book V, are guarding the gate together: an older warrior and a beautiful youth bound by love.
body: Conington remarks that they are introduced as if they had not been named before, though they appeared in the foot-race at 5.294-361, where Nisus slipped and tripped a rival so that Euryalus could win. Their relationship is modelled on Greek pairs of an older lover and a younger beloved (compare Achilles and Patroclus), and Virgil presents it with tenderness: 'one love' (amor unus) united them. Conington takes amor unus as a compound of 'one mind' (mens una) and reciprocal love (amor reciprocus). The night expedition that follows is modelled on the Doloneia of Iliad 10, where Diomedes and Odysseus raid the Trojan camp at night; but Virgil's version ends in disaster rather than success, and Euryalus' greed for spoils is the cause.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.176 (Nisus and Euryalus introduced afresh; and on 9.182, amor unus)
Virgil, Aeneid 5.294 (the foot-race), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Homer, Iliad 10.220 (Diomedes volunteers for the night raid)

anchor: fatal passion become a proper god
title: 'Dira cupido': divine impulse or human desire?
greek: dine hunc ardorem mentibus addunt, / Euryale, an sua cuique deus fit dira cupido?
short: Nisus wonders whether the gods put this burning desire into his mind, or whether each man's own fierce desire becomes his god.
body: This is one of the most searching questions in the Aeneid, raising the problem of double motivation familiar from Homer: are human actions caused by gods or by people themselves? Heyne, cited by Conington, saw the germ in Odyssey 4.712; Taubmann, cited by Conington, compares a line of Menander (Gnomai Monostichoi 434) that makes each person's mind a god; Conington himself notes that dira cupido here carries no blame, though it describes longing that overpowers reason. Nisus' words anticipate what goes wrong: his longing for a great deed (and Euryalus' later lust for slaughter and booty) leads to both deaths. Readers often link the question to the poem's wider exploration of furor, passion that the gods exploit but humans own.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.184 (dirane sua cuique deus fit cupido; Od. 4.712)
Homer, Odyssey 4.712 (Medon: some god or his own heart urged him)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.184, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Rhamnes, the augur who did not foresee
greek: rex idem et regi Turno gratissimus augur, / sed non augurio potuit depellere pestem
short: Nisus' first victim is Rhamnes, a king and Turnus' favourite augur, killed in his drunken sleep: his prophetic skill could not save him.
body: The line has the sharp irony Virgil uses for the deaths of priests and seers (compare Panthus in 2.429-430). An augur interprets the will of the gods from birds and signs, yet Rhamnes cannot foresee his own death. The night raid is grimly realistic: Rutulians lie sprawled among chariots, armour and wine, and Serranus is killed after gambling late into the night ('happy, had he played out the night'). The slaughter is compared to a starving lion raging through a sheepfold (9.339-341), which recalls the wolf simile for Turnus at 9.59-66: now the Trojans are the predators. The killing of sleeping men follows Diomedes' slaughter of the sleeping Thracians in Iliad 10.482-497.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 9.324, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Homer, Iliad 10.482 (Diomedes kills the sleeping Thracians)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. augur

title: The fatal spoils: Rhamnes' belt and Messapus' helmet
greek: Euryalus phaleras Rhamnetis et aurea bullis / cingula ... / tum galeam Messapi habilem cristisque decoram / induit
short: Euryalus takes Rhamnes' gold-studded belt and Messapus' plumed helmet; the helmet's glitter in the moonlight betrays him to Volscens' horsemen.
body: Stripping the dead of arms was normal heroic practice, but in the Aeneid it often brings doom. Virgil traces the belt's history, a gift from Caedicus to Remulus of Tibur and then a Rutulian prize, to show how such objects pass from hand to hand. The helmet 'forgotten' in its glitter (galea ... sublustri noctis in umbra, 9.373-374) gives Euryalus away. Readers connect this with Turnus taking Pallas' sword-belt in Book X (10.495-505), which costs him his life at the end of Book XII. Nisus had warned that 'vengeance is sated'; Euryalus' greed (Mackail's 'excess of murderous desire') makes the cupido of 9.185 concrete.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 9.359, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. cingulum

title: Nisus' prayer to the Moon (Diana)
greek: tu, dea, tu praesens nostro succurre labori, / astrorum decus et nemorum Latonia custos
short: Before his first throw, Nisus prays to the Moon as Diana, 'Latonian goddess, glory of the stars and guardian of the woodlands'.
body: Diana is the daughter of Latona (Greek Leto) and sister of Apollo; as huntress she guards the woods, and she is identified with the Moon (Luna). Nisus, son of the huntress Ida (9.177), appeals to her as a hunter who has hung trophies of the chase in her temple. The prayer follows the regular structure of ancient prayer: invocation with titles, claims on the god based on past offerings (the 'da ut dem' principle of reciprocity), then request. It is answered at once: his spears kill Sulmo and Tagus. But the success only provokes Volscens to kill Euryalus, so the divine help is real yet useless, a recurring pattern in the poem.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid 9.403, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. Latona (Latonia)
Catullus 34 (hymn to Diana, addressed as Latonia and Luna)

anchor: I am here, I did it
title: 'Me, me, adsum qui feci'
greek: me, me, adsum qui feci, in me convertite ferrum, / o Rutuli!
short: Nisus reveals himself to save Euryalus: 'On me, on me, I am here, I did it, on me turn your steel, O Rutulians!' He is too late.
body: The broken, repeated pronoun conveys panic and love. Conington quotes Taubmann that the doubled me shows Nisus struggling to get the words out, and calls adsum qui feci a confession, comparing the formula fecit in inscriptions. Nisus' plea for his friend's innocence ('he only loved his hapless friend too well') is one of the most quoted lines of the poem. The line's emotional power has made it a model for later scenes of self-sacrifice; it also contrasts with the cold efficiency of the earlier slaughter. Nisus then kills Volscens and dies on his friend's body, finding 'the quiet sleep of death'.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.427 (me, me, adsum qui feci; Taubmann)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.427, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. adsum

title: The dying Euryalus as a cut flower and a poppy
greek: purpureus veluti cum flos succisus aratro / languescit moriens, lassove papavera collo / demisere caput pluvia cum forte gravantur
short: Euryalus' head droops in death like a purple flower cut by the plough or poppies bowing their heads under a sudden rain.
body: Conington traces the two images to famous models: Catullus' flower on the meadow's edge touched by the passing plough (11.21-24), and the poppy in Iliad 8.306-308, which droops its head under its seed and spring rain, used for the dying Gorgythion. He also cites Apollonius 3.1398 ff. The beauty of the youth is emphasised in death; the eroticised language of Catullus (where the flower is the poet's love) suits the bond of Nisus and Euryalus. The same flower image returns for Pallas' corpse (11.68-71). The juxtaposition of beauty and violence is typical of Virgil's handling of young deaths.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.435 (Catullus; Il. 8.306 ff.; Apollonius 3.1398)
Homer, Iliad 8.306 (the poppy simile for Gorgythion)
Catullus 11.21-24 (the flower touched by the plough)

title: 'Fortunati ambo': the poet's promise of fame
greek: Fortunati ambo! si quid mea carmina possunt, / nulla dies umquam memori vos eximet aevo, / dum domus Aeneae Capitoli immobile saxum / accolet imperiumque pater Romanus habebit
short: Virgil speaks in his own voice: if his poetry has any power, the two friends will be remembered as long as Rome stands on the Capitol.
body: Such direct authorial apostrophes are rare in the Aeneid, which makes this one striking. The fame (kleos) of Homeric heroes depended on song; Virgil claims that power for his own poem and ties it to Rome's permanence. Conington reads 'the house of Aeneas' as both the Julian family and the Roman people, and the Mackail's 'stedfast stone' of the Capitoline as an image of the empire's duration. The 'lord of Rome' (pater Romanus) has been interpreted as Augustus and his successors, as the Roman citizen-father, or as Capitoline Jupiter; Conington reviews these views and prefers a combination of the first two. The promise has proved truer than Rome's empire itself.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.446 (Fortunati ambo; Capitoli immobile saxum; pater Romanus)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.446, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Horace, Odes 3.30.8-9 (fame lasting while the pontiff climbs the Capitol)

anchor: the heads of Euryalus and Nisus
title: The heads on spears
greek: quin ipsa arrectis (visu miserabile) in hastis / praefigunt capita et multo clamore sequuntur / Euryali et Nisi
short: At dawn the Rutulians parade the severed heads of Nisus and Euryalus on spears before the Trojan walls.
body: Mutilating the dead was a mark of savagery in ancient war; in Homer threats to behead and display a corpse are made (Hector's threat for Patroclus, Iliad 18.176-177), but rarely carried out. Conington notes that some editors suspected line 467 but that the names are clearly needed for the effect. The narrator's parenthesis 'pitiable sight' (visu miserabile) gives the Trojans' view. The scene also fulfils Nisus' wish (9.213-215) for burial or a tomb, cruelly denied. It leads directly to the lament of Euryalus' mother, who learns the news from Rumour.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.466 (praefigunt capita; line 467 defended)
Homer, Iliad 18.176 (Hector wants to set Patroclus' head on a stake)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.465, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

anchor: the shuttle starts from her hand
title: The lament of Euryalus' mother
greek: excussi manibus radii revolutaque pensa
short: Euryalus' mother, the only Trojan woman who chose to follow the army rather than stay in Sicily, drops her weaving at the news and laments on the walls.
body: The shuttle (radius) falling from her hand recalls Andromache, who drops her shuttle when she hears the wailing for Hector (Iliad 22.437-448). Her lament follows the ritual structure of the Homeric goos: address to the dead, reproach for abandoning her, grief at the lack of proper burial (she could not close his eyes, wash his wounds or dress him in the robe she was weaving), and a wish to die. Earlier Euryalus had asked Ascanius to care for her because he could not bear her tears (9.284-292). Her grief undermines the Trojans' courage, and she is carried away, a sign that private sorrow has no place on the battle line.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 22.437 (Andromache drops her shuttle)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.473, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. radius

title: The testudo (tortoise formation)
greek: accelerant acta pariter testudine Volsci
short: The Volscians advance on the Trojan rampart under a testudo, a roof of shields locked overhead like a tortoise's shell.
body: The testudo was a Roman siege technique: soldiers raised their shields above their heads, overlapping like tiles, to protect themselves from missiles while they filled ditches or undermined walls. Conington ties the phrase to the testudo at Priam's palace (2.441) and to Iliad 12.378 ff. Its presence in a heroic-age battle is an anachronism, typical of Virgil's habit of describing early Italy in terms of Roman warfare. The defenders answer in kind with long poles and a huge rolled stone that breaks the shell apart. The Trojan camp, a fortified 'city', turns Book IX into a siege like the Iliad's attack on the Greek wall (Iliad 12), with the roles reversed: the Trojans now defend a wall against invaders.

sources.cite: C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. testudo
Virgil, Aeneid 9.505, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Homer, Iliad 12.1 (the Trojan assault on the Greek wall)

title: Invocation of Calliope and the Muses
greek: Vos, o Calliope, precor, aspirate canenti / quas ibi tum ferro strages, quae funera Turnus / ediderit
short: Before Turnus' slaughter Virgil asks Calliope and her sister Muses to inspire him and to 'unroll the broad borders of war'.
body: Calliope is the chief of the nine Muses, as Hesiod says (Theogony 79), and patron of epic. The plural vos ('you, O Calliope') means Calliope with her sisters (Mackail: 'Thy sisterhood, O Calliope'); compare the Muse-invocation before a battle in Iliad 14.508. The phrase 'oras evolvite belli' ('unroll the broad borders of war') is commonly heard as an echo of Ennius' Annales. The image is of unrolling a book-scroll, or of opening up the full extent of the war. Such invocations mark major battle-sequences; compare Erato at 7.37 and the Helicon invocation at 7.641. Lines 9.528-529 repeat the formula of 7.645-646 on the Muses' knowledge and mortal rumour.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.525 (Il. 14.508; Hesiod, Theog. 79; Ennius, oras evolvere belli)
Hesiod, Theogony 79 (Calliope, foremost of the Muses)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.525, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: The eagle and the wolf of Mars
greek: qualis ubi aut leporem aut candenti corpore cycnum / sustulit alta petens pedibus Iovis armiger uncis, / quaesitum aut matri multis balatibus agnum / Martius a stabulis rapuit lupus
short: Turnus tearing Lycus and part of the wall away is like Jupiter's eagle carrying off a hare or a swan, or Mars' wolf snatching a lamb.
body: 'Jove's armour-bearer' (Iovis armiger) is the eagle, which carried Jupiter's thunderbolt; Horace calls it 'the winged minister of the thunderbolt' (Odes 4.4.1). The wolf was sacred to Mars, as the she-wolf of Rome's founding shows. The model is Hector swooping like an eagle on a lamb or a hare (Iliad 22.308-310). The double simile emphasises Turnus' power and his predatory nature, and the bleating lamb sought by its mother picks up the pathos of the lamb image from 9.59-66. Note how the same Martian wolf could stand for Rome's founding (8.630-634) and for its enemy's violence.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 22.308 (Hector like an eagle seizing a lamb or hare)
Horace, Odes 4.4.1 (the eagle as 'ministrum fulminis')
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. armiger

title: Numanus Remulus: Italian hardness and Phrygian softness
greek: non pudet obsidione iterum valloque teneri, / bis capti Phryges ... / durum a stirpe genus ... / o vere Phrygiae, neque enim Phryges
short: Turnus' brother-in-law Numanus Remulus taunts the Trojans as effeminate Easterners, contrasting the hard life of Italian farmers and hunters.
body: Conington explains 'twice taken' as the two sacks of Troy, by Hercules under Laomedon and by the Greeks. Numanus' speech is a little ethnography: Italians dip newborns in icy rivers, hunt as boys, farm with spears in hand and fight into old age. The Trojans wear saffron and purple, sleeved tunics and the Phrygian mitra with ribbons, love dancing, and worship Cybele on Mount Dindymus to the music of the double flute and the Berecyntian boxwood pipe. Conington notes that these are mainly post-Homeric stereotypes and that the scorn of dancing reflects Roman attitudes of Virgil's own time. The speech echoes Virgil's praise of Italy (Georgics 2.167-172), so the Italian values are partly endorsed, yet the boaster dies at once, shot by a boy.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.599 (bis capti; and notes on 9.603-619, mitra, Dindyma, buxus)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.598, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)
Virgil, Aeneid 6.784 (Berecyntian Mother), Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

title: Thunder on the left: a good omen
greek: audiit et caeli genitor de parte serena / intonuit laevum
short: Ascanius prays to Jupiter, vowing a white bull with gilded horns; Jupiter thunders on the left from a clear sky, and the boy's arrow kills Remulus.
body: In Roman augury, signs on the left were favourable, while Greek practice treated the right as lucky; Cicero discusses the difference (De Divinatione 2.82). Conington notes that left-side thunder is a good omen here as at 2.693, where Jupiter confirms the flame on Ascanius' head. Thunder from a clear sky was an especially strong sign. The vowed victim, a young steer as tall as its mother, with gilded horns, follows Roman and Homeric custom (Odyssey 3.432 ff. on gilding the horns). This is Ascanius' first kill in war, and his retort to the dead man, 'Phrygians twice taken return this answer to Rutulians', shows a new maturity.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, The Works of Virgil with a Commentary, Aeneid VII-XII (London; Perseus digital text of the 1876 edition), note on Aen. 9.631 (intonuit laevum; cf. 2.693; and on 9.627, gilded horns)
Cicero, De Divinatione 2.82 (left-hand signs favourable for Romans)
Virgil, Aeneid 9.630, Latin text ed. J. B. Greenough (1900)

anchor: this is the way to heaven
title: 'Macte nova virtute, puer: sic itur ad astra'
greek: macte nova virtute, puer, sic itur ad astra, / dis genite et geniture deos
short: Apollo praises Ascanius' first kill as 'the way to the stars', hails him as son and father of gods, then forbids him to fight further.
body: Macte is a ritual word of approval, originally used in sacrifice ('be honoured'). 'The way to heaven' (sic itur ad astra, literally 'to the stars') became proverbial for the road to glory. Conington reads 'parent of gods to be' as pointing to the deified Caesars, and 'nor art thou bounded in a Troy' as a prophecy with several fulfilments: the move from the Trojan camp to Lavinium and Alba, and Rome's expansion over the world. Apollo then disguises himself as old Butes, Anchises' armour-bearer, a device Conington traces to Iliad 17.322 (Apollo disguised as Periphas). Protecting Ascanius matters for fate: the line of Iulus must survive to reach Augustus.

title: The storm simile: the rainy Kids
greek: quantus ab occasu veniens pluvialibus Haedis / verberat imber humum
short: The missiles fall as heavily as rain lashing the ground when the rainy Kids set, or hail when Jupiter breaks up the storm-clouds.
body: The Haedi ('Kids') are two stars in the constellation Auriga, the Charioteer. Their setting and rising marked seasons of storms at sea, especially in autumn; Horace speaks of the violent onset of the rising Kid (Odes 3.1.28), a parallel Conington cites, along with Georgics 1.205. Conington also notes that the Homeric model (Iliad 12.278-286) compares a shower of stones to a snowstorm. Such astronomical lore was familiar to Roman farmers and sailors, and to readers of Aratus' Phaenomena. The simile takes the battle out of the camp into the whole sky.

title: Pandarus and Bitias, the twin oaks at the gate
greek: quales aeriae liquentia flumina circum / sive Padi ripis Athesim seu propter amoenum / consurgunt geminae quercus
short: Two giant brothers, Pandarus and Bitias, open the gate in defiance of Aeneas' orders and stand on either side like twin oaks on the banks of the Po or Adige.
body: Conington shows that the scene is modelled on Iliad 12.127 ff., where the Lapiths Polypoetes and Leonteus stand at the gate of the Greek wall like two oaks on a mountain (12.132), and adds that Macrobius linked it to an episode in Ennius' Histrian war. He notes that Homer's comparison is about firmness, Virgil's about height. The Padus (Po) and Athesis (Adige) are rivers of northern Italy, Virgil's own homeland, so the Trojan giants are given an Italian simile. Their foolhardy act lets Turnus in: Bitias is felled by a huge spear (9.703-709) and Pandarus, shutting the gate, traps Turnus inside with the Trojans.

title: Bitias' fall and the pier at Baiae
greek: talis in Euboico Baiarum litore quondam / saxea pila cadit ... / tum sonitu Prochyta alta tremit durumque cubile / Inarime Iovis imperiis imposta Typhoeo
short: Bitias' crash is compared to a mass of masonry dropped into the sea at Baiae to build a pier, which makes the islands of Prochyta and Inarime tremble.
body: Conington notes how unusual it is for Virgil to draw a simile from contemporary practice: the Romans built harbours and villas on the Bay of Naples by sinking great concrete piers (pilae) into the sea, which Horace also describes. Baiae is called 'Euboean' because nearby Cumae was founded from Chalcis in Euboea (compare 6.2). Prochyta is modern Procida. Inarime (Ischia) is said to lie on the giant Typhoeus, whom Jupiter buried beneath it; Conington explains that Virgil identified Homer's 'Arima' (ein Arimois, Iliad 2.783, the site of Typhoeus' bed) with the island, as some ancient scholars did, perhaps misreading the phrase as one word. The giant motif suits the fall of a giant warrior.

title: 'Here too an Achilles': Turnus and Pandarus
greek: hic etiam inventum Priamo narrabis Achillem
short: Shut inside the camp, Turnus tells Pandarus he can report to Priam in the underworld that here too an Achilles has been found, then splits his head in two.
body: Turnus deliberately takes the role of Achilles, which the Sibyl had predicted ('another Achilles, born in Latium', 6.89); Conington compares that line and 2.547, where Pyrrhus mockingly sends Priam to report to his father Achilles. Pandarus shares the name of the Trojan archer of the Iliad. Turnus' smile and composure (sedato pectore) contrast with Pandarus' rage. But Turnus then makes a fatal error: in 'rage and mad thirst of slaughter' he forgets to open the gates for his army, and the narrator says that had he done so, 'that had been the last day of the war and of the nation' (9.757-759). His heroism is real, but his furor undoes him.

title: Turnus retreating like a lion
greek: ceu saevum turba leonem / cum telis premit infensis; at territus ille, / asper, acerba tuens, retro redit
short: Rallied by Mnestheus, the Trojans force Turnus slowly back, like a lion pressed by hunters, too proud to turn and flee, too hard-pressed to attack.
body: Conington identifies the model as Ajax's slow retreat before the Trojans in Iliad 11.544 ff., where Ajax is compared to a lion driven from a cattle-yard by men and dogs and then to a stubborn donkey; Virgil keeps the lion and its unwillingness to retreat. The phrase asper, acerba tuens ('fierce, glaring grimly') comes from Lucretius (5.33). Turnus, the predator wolf of 9.59-66 and the tiger of 9.730, now becomes the hunted beast. Juno cannot help him, because Jupiter has sent Iris to forbid it (9.802-805), a reminder that Turnus' success depends on divine permission.

anchor: About the hollows of his temples
title: Turnus under the storm of missiles: Ennius and Homer
greek: ergo nec clipeo iuvenis subsistere tantum / nec dextra valet ... strepit adsiduo cava tempora circum / tinnitu galea
short: Turnus' helmet rings with endless blows, his crest is torn away and sweat pours from him: a passage imitated from Homer through the early Roman poet Ennius.
body: Conington shows a chain of imitation. In Iliad 16.102-111 Ajax, pressed at the ships, can barely hold his ground: his helmet rings with blows, his shoulder tires under the shield and sweat pours from him. Ennius adapted this for a Roman tribune fighting in the Histrian war (in the Annales, in his account of the Histrian war), and Conington quotes Ennius' line on missiles converging 'like rain on the tribune'. Virgil reworks both. The double allusion places Turnus in a line of heroic last stands, Greek and Roman. Readers who know Ennius' tribune would see Turnus as an Italian hero fighting with Roman endurance. Macrobius (Saturnalia 6.3) discusses Virgil's borrowings from Ennius in this way.

Homer, Iliad 16.102 (Ajax under a hail of missiles)

anchor: leapt fully armed into the river
title: Turnus' leap into the Tiber
greek: tum demum praeceps saltu sese omnibus armis / in fluvium dedit. ille suo cum gurgite flavo / accepit venientem ac mollibus extulit undis
short: Exhausted, Turnus leaps fully armed into the Tiber, which receives him in its yellow eddies and carries him back to his comrades, washed clean of slaughter.
body: The book ends not with Turnus' defeat but with his escape. Conington suggests that Virgil may have followed a description of Horatius Cocles, who swam the Tiber in armour after holding the bridge (Livy 2.10; shown on the shield at 8.650); he notes that line 816 echoes Ennius ('Teque, pater Tiberine') and that mollibus means 'buoyant'. The Tiber, which had welcomed Aeneas as its destined lord (8.31-78), here helps the Italian hero, a reminder that Turnus too belongs to this land. The washing away of blood (abluta caede) gives a moment of cleansing before the battles of Book X.
